topics.title: Murasaki Shikibu and the World's First Novel

hook.text: The world's first novel was written by a woman in eleventh-century Japan, a thousand years before the modern novel emerged.

buildup.text: Murasaki Shikibu was a lady-in-waiting at the imperial court who wrote The Tale of Genji around the year 1000.

discovery.text: Genji explores psychological depth, romantic complexity, and the passage of time with a sophistication unmatched for centuries.

twist.text: We do not even know her real name. 'Murasaki Shikibu' is a nickname, and her identity remains partially a mystery.

climax.text: She invented the novel as a literary form, proving that women were creating groundbreaking literature a millennium ago.

punchline.text: A woman invented the novel a thousand years before anyone noticed.

quiz.question: What literary milestone is attributed to Murasaki Shikibu?
options: She wrote the first autobiography in world literature
She wrote the world's first novel, The Tale of Genji
She created the first dictionary of the Japanese language

topics.title: Christine de Pizan: Europe's First Professional Woman Writer

hook.text: In 1405, Christine de Pizan wrote the first feminist work in European history and supported her family with her pen.

buildup.text: After her husband died, she became Europe's first woman to earn a living as a professional writer.

discovery.text: The Book of the City of Ladies built an imaginary city populated by history's greatest women to defend female worth.

twist.text: Male scholars attacked her, but she debated them publicly in writing, becoming Europe's first literary feminist voice.

climax.text: Christine proved that women could be public intellectuals six centuries before the word 'feminism' was coined.

punchline.text: She built a city of women six hundred years before feminism.

quiz.question: What distinction does Christine de Pizan hold in European history?
options: She was the first woman to attend a European university
She was Europe's first woman to earn a living as a professional writer
She was the first woman elected to a European parliament

topics.title: Jane Austen's Quiet Revolution

hook.text: Jane Austen published all her novels anonymously, credited only as 'By a Lady,' and died unknown to the wider public.

buildup.text: Her novels dissect class, money, and marriage with an irony so sharp it still cuts two centuries later.

discovery.text: Austen invented free indirect discourse in English fiction, letting readers hear characters' thoughts without quotation marks.

twist.text: Critics dismissed her as a writer of domestic romances for decades before scholars recognized her radical formal innovations.

climax.text: Austen proved that novels about women's lives were not minor literature but the foundation of the modern novel.

punchline.text: She revolutionized fiction without ever putting her name on it.

quiz.question: What narrative technique did Austen pioneer in English fiction?
options: The unreliable narrator
Free indirect discourse
Stream of consciousness

topics.title: The Brontë Sisters and the Power of Pseudonyms

hook.text: Three sisters in a remote Yorkshire parsonage published under male names and changed English literature forever.

buildup.text: Charlotte, Emily, and Anne Brontë became Currer, Ellis, and Acton Bell to be taken seriously in a male-dominated field.

discovery.text: Emily's Wuthering Heights was called 'savage' and 'brutal.' Charlotte's Jane Eyre was an instant sensation.

twist.text: When their identities were revealed, critics who had praised the novels suddenly questioned their quality.

climax.text: The Brontës proved that gender bias in publishing was real and that pseudonyms could subvert it.

punchline.text: They hid behind male names to prove female genius.

quiz.question: How did critics react when the Brontës' real identities were revealed?
options: They celebrated the sisters as groundbreaking women authors
Critics who had praised the novels suddenly questioned their quality
They had already guessed the authors were women

topics.title: George Eliot: The Woman Behind the Man's Name

hook.text: George Eliot was not a man. She was Mary Ann Evans, one of the most brilliant minds in Victorian England.

buildup.text: She adopted a male pen name because she wanted her fiction judged by its quality, not dismissed as 'lady's writing.'

discovery.text: Middlemarch is considered by many critics to be the greatest English novel, with its vast psychological and social scope.

twist.text: She lived openly with a married man, scandalizing Victorian society, yet her novels championed moral complexity over judgment.

climax.text: Eliot proved that a woman could write the most intellectually ambitious novel in the English language.

punchline.text: The greatest English novel was written by a woman in disguise.

quiz.question: Why did Mary Ann Evans use the pen name George Eliot?
options: She admired a male author named George Eliot
She wanted her fiction judged by quality, not dismissed as 'lady's writing'
Her publisher required all authors to use pseudonyms

topics.title: Phillis Wheatley: The Enslaved Poet Who Amazed the World

hook.text: Phillis Wheatley was kidnapped from Africa, enslaved in Boston, and became the first African American to publish a book.

buildup.text: Her 1773 book of poems astonished readers who could not believe an enslaved Black woman could write sophisticated verse.

discovery.text: She had to defend her authorship before a panel of eighteen white men who examined her to prove she actually wrote her poems.

twist.text: Thomas Jefferson dismissed her work, revealing that even Enlightenment thinkers could not overcome their racial prejudice.

climax.text: Wheatley's mere existence as a published poet challenged the entire intellectual justification for slavery in America.

punchline.text: She wrote her way into a history that tried to erase her.

quiz.question: Why did Wheatley have to appear before a panel of eighteen men?
options: To receive a literary prize for her poetry
To prove she had actually written her own poems
To request permission to publish from colonial authorities

topics.title: Mary Wollstonecraft and the Rights of Women

hook.text: Mary Wollstonecraft wrote the founding text of feminism in 1792 and was vilified for it for over a century.

buildup.text: A Vindication of the Rights of Woman argued that women are not naturally inferior but are made so by lack of education.

discovery.text: She wrote it in just six weeks, furious that the French Revolution's 'rights of man' excluded half of humanity.

twist.text: After her death, her husband published her private life, and scandalized readers dismissed her ideas for a hundred years.

climax.text: Wollstonecraft's argument — that education, not nature, determines ability — became the foundation of all feminist thought.

punchline.text: She wrote feminism's founding text in six furious weeks.

quiz.question: What was Wollstonecraft's central argument in her Vindication?
options: Women should have the right to vote in elections
Women are not naturally inferior but are made so by lack of education
Women and men should live in separate societies

topics.title: Harriet Beecher Stowe and Uncle Tom's Cabin

hook.text: Lincoln reportedly told Stowe, 'So you're the little woman who wrote the book that started this great war.'

buildup.text: Uncle Tom's Cabin sold three hundred thousand copies in its first year and made the horrors of slavery viscerally real.

discovery.text: Stowe translated abolitionist arguments from political abstraction into emotional stories that ordinary readers could feel.

twist.text: Southern states banned the book. Some made it a crime to own a copy, proving how much they feared its power.

climax.text: Stowe proved that a novel by a woman could shift national politics and accelerate the march toward war and freedom.

punchline.text: One woman's novel helped start the war that ended slavery.

quiz.question: How did Southern states react to Uncle Tom's Cabin?
options: They praised it as a fair depiction of plantation life
They banned it and made it a crime to own a copy
They ignored it as irrelevant fiction

topics.title: Louisa May Alcott's Little Women

hook.text: Louisa May Alcott did not want to write Little Women. Her publisher insisted, and she wrote it under protest.

buildup.text: The novel follows the four March sisters growing up during the Civil War, navigating ambition, love, and independence.

discovery.text: Jo March, the tomboyish writer, became literature's first aspirational female character for millions of young women.

twist.text: Alcott hated the conventional marriage ending but wrote it because her publisher demanded Jo marry someone.

climax.text: Little Women showed that stories about girls' inner lives could be universal literature, not niche entertainment.

punchline.text: She wrote it under protest, and it became immortal.

quiz.question: Why did Alcott write the marriage ending reluctantly?
options: She wanted Jo to marry a different character
Her publisher demanded Jo marry someone despite Alcott's objections
She believed the story needed a tragic ending instead

topics.title: Kate Chopin's The Awakening

hook.text: Kate Chopin's The Awakening was so scandalous in 1899 that it destroyed her career and was forgotten for sixty years.

buildup.text: The novel follows Edna Pontellier, a married woman who discovers her own desires and refuses to suppress them any longer.

discovery.text: Chopin dared to portray a woman choosing personal freedom over motherhood and marriage, shocking Victorian readers.

twist.text: The novel was rediscovered in the 1960s by feminist scholars and is now considered a masterpiece of American literature.

climax.text: Chopin's career was destroyed because she told the truth about women's inner lives sixty years too early.

punchline.text: The truth she told in 1899 only became acceptable in 1969.

quiz.question: What happened to Chopin's career after publishing The Awakening?
options: She became America's most celebrated author
The scandal destroyed her career and the book was forgotten for sixty years
She was invited to lecture at universities across America

topics.title: Nella Larsen and the Harlem Renaissance

hook.text: Nella Larsen wrote two brilliant novels about race and identity, then vanished from literature to work as a nurse.

buildup.text: Quicksand and Passing explored the psychological cost of living between racial identities in 1920s America.

discovery.text: Passing follows two light-skinned Black women, one who 'passes' as white, forging a bond charged with envy and danger.

twist.text: Larsen was falsely accused of plagiarism, and the humiliation drove her out of the literary world permanently.

climax.text: Larsen's rediscovery showed how racism and sexism conspired to silence one of America's most perceptive voices.

punchline.text: The literary world lost her, but her novels outlived the silence.

quiz.question: Why did Larsen stop writing literature?
options: She lost interest in fiction and pursued science
A false accusation of plagiarism drove her from the literary world
Her publisher refused to print works by Black women

topics.title: Charlotte Perkins Gilman's The Yellow Wallpaper

hook.text: Charlotte Perkins Gilman wrote a horror story about wallpaper that became one of feminism's most important texts.

buildup.text: The story follows a woman confined to a room by her doctor husband, slowly descending into madness as she stares at the wallpaper.

discovery.text: Gilman wrote it from personal experience after a doctor prescribed 'rest cure' that nearly drove her insane.

twist.text: She sent the story to the doctor who had treated her. He never responded, but reportedly changed his treatment methods.

climax.text: The Yellow Wallpaper exposed how medicine and marriage could imprison women's minds under the guise of care.

punchline.text: A horror story about wallpaper changed how doctors treat women.

quiz.question: What inspired Gilman to write The Yellow Wallpaper?
options: A nightmare she had about a haunted house
Her personal experience with a 'rest cure' that nearly drove her insane
A news article about women in psychiatric asylums

topics.title: Virginia Woolf and Stream of Consciousness

hook.text: Virginia Woolf declared that 'a woman must have money and a room of her own if she is to write fiction.'

buildup.text: She pioneered stream of consciousness in novels like Mrs Dalloway and To the Lighthouse, capturing thought's fluid motion.

discovery.text: Woolf argued in A Room of One's Own that women's literary absence was caused by poverty and exclusion, not lack of talent.

twist.text: She suffered from severe mental illness throughout her life and drowned herself in 1941, leaving a devastating farewell letter.

climax.text: Woolf transformed both the novel's form and the conversation about why women had been excluded from literature.

punchline.text: She rewrote the novel and explained why women could not.

quiz.question: What did Woolf argue caused women's literary absence?
options: Women lacked the natural talent for fiction writing
Poverty and exclusion, not lack of talent
Women preferred other art forms over literature

topics.title: Zora Neale Hurston's Their Eyes Were Watching God

hook.text: Zora Neale Hurston wrote a masterpiece that was forgotten for decades until Alice Walker literally found her unmarked grave.

buildup.text: Their Eyes Were Watching God follows Janie Crawford's journey through three marriages toward self-discovery and freedom.

discovery.text: Hurston wrote in the vernacular of Black Southern speech, preserving voices that literary fiction had ignored.

twist.text: Richard Wright attacked the novel for not being political enough, and it fell out of print for thirty years.

climax.text: Hurston proved that Black women's interior lives were worthy of literary attention and lyrical beauty.

punchline.text: A lost masterpiece waited thirty years for someone to listen.

quiz.question: How was Hurston's Their Eyes Were Watching God rediscovered?
options: A university professor found it in a used bookshop
Alice Walker searched for Hurston's unmarked grave and championed her work
A Hollywood studio adapted it into a film

topics.title: Simone de Beauvoir's The Second Sex

hook.text: Simone de Beauvoir wrote 'One is not born, but rather becomes, a woman' — one sentence that transformed feminist thought.

buildup.text: The Second Sex, published in 1949, examined how society constructs femininity and confines women to the role of 'Other.'

discovery.text: Beauvoir argued that gender is not biology but a social construction, anticipating decades of feminist and gender theory.

twist.text: The Vatican placed the book on its Index of Forbidden Books, and critics called it immoral and dangerous.

climax.text: The Second Sex became the intellectual foundation of second-wave feminism and remains essential reading worldwide.

punchline.text: One sentence rewrote how the world understood gender.

quiz.question: What was Beauvoir's revolutionary argument about gender?
options: Women are biologically superior to men
Gender is not biology but a social construction
Men and women should live in entirely separate societies

topics.title: Flannery O'Connor's Southern Gothic

hook.text: Flannery O'Connor raised peacocks on a Georgia farm and wrote some of the most violent, funny stories in American literature.

buildup.text: Her stories feature grotesque characters, sudden violence, and moments of divine grace erupting through ordinary Southern life.

discovery.text: O'Connor said she wrote about the grotesque because 'for the hard of hearing you shout, and for the almost blind you draw large.'

twist.text: She wrote her greatest work while dying of lupus, producing masterpieces in the years she knew would be her last.

climax.text: O'Connor proved that a Catholic woman in rural Georgia could write stories that stand with the best in world literature.

punchline.text: She wrote with one eye on eternity and the other on peacocks.

quiz.question: Why did O'Connor write about grotesque characters and violence?
options: She believed Southern life was inherently violent
She said 'for the hard of hearing you shout, and for the almost blind you draw large'
Her publisher demanded sensational content

topics.title: Clarice Lispector's Interior Revolution

hook.text: Clarice Lispector published her first novel at twenty-three and was immediately hailed as a genius in Brazil.

buildup.text: Her fiction explores consciousness itself: the moment a housewife sees a cockroach becomes a metaphysical crisis.

discovery.text: Lispector wrote in a style so unique that critics compare her to Kafka, Woolf, and Borges — but she resembles none of them.

twist.text: She was largely unknown outside Brazil until translations in the 2010s revealed her to English-speaking readers as a master.

climax.text: Lispector proved that women's domestic experience could be the raw material for the most radical literary experimentation.

punchline.text: She turned a woman staring at a cockroach into philosophy.

quiz.question: Why was Lispector largely unknown outside Brazil for decades?
options: Her work was banned by the Brazilian government
Translations into English did not appear until the 2010s
She refused to allow her work to be translated

topics.title: Carson McCullers and the Lonely Heart

hook.text: Carson McCullers published her first novel at twenty-three and was hailed as a genius of American loneliness.

buildup.text: The Heart Is a Lonely Hunter follows misfits in a small Georgia town who pour their souls into a deaf-mute man.

discovery.text: McCullers wrote about isolation, queerness, and racial injustice in the Deep South decades before others dared.

twist.text: She suffered strokes in her twenties that left her partially paralyzed, yet she kept writing through immense pain.

climax.text: McCullers proved that the literature of loneliness could be as powerful as the literature of love.

punchline.text: She made loneliness the subject that American fiction needed.

quiz.question: What themes did McCullers explore decades before others?
options: Space travel and futuristic technology
Isolation, queerness, and racial injustice in the Deep South
European aristocratic society and manners

topics.title: Toni Morrison and the Black Experience in America

hook.text: Toni Morrison won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1993, becoming the first African American woman to receive the honor.

buildup.text: Her novel Beloved, based on a true story, explores a mother who kills her child rather than let her be returned to slavery.

discovery.text: Morrison said she wrote the books she wanted to read, because no one else was writing them for Black readers.

twist.text: Beloved was initially rejected by many critics and did not win the National Book Award, sparking outrage among Black writers.

climax.text: Morrison gave American literature a voice it had suppressed for centuries and proved that Black stories are universal stories.

punchline.text: She wrote the books nobody else would, and they changed everything.

quiz.question: Why did Morrison say she wrote her novels?
options: To educate white readers about Black history
She wrote the books she wanted to read, because no one else was writing them
To win literary prizes and critical recognition

topics.title: Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie and the Single Story

hook.text: Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie's TED Talk 'The Danger of a Single Story' has been viewed over thirty million times worldwide.

buildup.text: Her novels Americanah and Half of a Yellow Sun explore Nigerian identity, immigration, and the legacy of colonialism.

discovery.text: Adichie argues that reducing any people to a single narrative is a form of power that flattens complex human experience.

twist.text: Her essay 'We Should All Be Feminists' was sampled by Beyoncé, bringing literary feminism to a global pop audience.

climax.text: Adichie bridges literary fiction and popular culture, proving that serious ideas can reach audiences beyond the bookshelf.

punchline.text: A Nigerian novelist's feminism reached millions through Beyoncé.

quiz.question: How did Adichie's feminist essay reach a global pop audience?
options: It was adapted into a Hollywood film
Beyoncé sampled it in a song
It was taught in every American school

topics.title: Isabel Allende and Latin American Magical Realism

hook.text: Isabel Allende is the most widely read Spanish-language author alive, with over seventy-five million books sold worldwide.

buildup.text: The House of the Spirits weaves magical realism through three generations of Chilean women surviving political upheaval.

discovery.text: Allende began writing it as a letter to her dying grandfather and transformed personal grief into literary magic.

twist.text: Male critics dismissed her as an imitator of García Márquez, but her focus on women's stories was entirely original.

climax.text: Allende proved that Latin American magical realism could center women's experiences and reach a global readership.

punchline.text: A letter to her grandfather became seventy-five million books.

quiz.question: How did The House of the Spirits originate?
options: As a political essay about Chilean history
As a letter to Allende's dying grandfather
As a short story for a literary magazine

topics.title: Arundhati Roy and The God of Small Things

hook.text: Arundhati Roy won the Booker Prize with her first novel and then did not publish another for twenty years.

buildup.text: The God of Small Things explores caste, forbidden love, and childhood trauma in Kerala with poetic, shattered prose.

discovery.text: Roy's prose breaks grammar rules deliberately, mimicking how children perceive a world they cannot yet understand.

twist.text: Instead of writing more novels, she spent two decades as a political activist fighting for India's marginalized people.

climax.text: Roy showed that a single novel can be enough to change literature and that a writer's duty extends beyond the page.

punchline.text: One novel was enough. She had a world to fight for.

quiz.question: Why did Roy wait twenty years to publish a second novel?
options: She suffered from severe writer's block
She spent two decades as a political activist for India's marginalized people
Publishers refused to print a follow-up to her debut

topics.title: Angela Carter and Feminist Fairy Tales

hook.text: Angela Carter rewrote fairy tales as feminist horror stories and changed how the world reads Little Red Riding Hood.

buildup.text: The Bloody Chamber reimagines classic fairy tales, exposing the violence, desire, and power hidden in children's stories.

discovery.text: Carter argued that fairy tales were not innocent. They taught girls to be passive, obedient, and afraid of their own power.

twist.text: Male critics called her work vulgar and sensational. Female readers recognized it as revolutionary and liberating.

climax.text: Carter proved that rewriting old stories is a radical act, because changing the story changes the world it describes.

punchline.text: She gave Little Red Riding Hood the teeth to bite back.

quiz.question: What did Carter argue fairy tales traditionally taught girls?
options: To be brave adventurers and independent thinkers
To be passive, obedient, and afraid of their own power
To value education and intellectual achievement

topics.title: Ursula K. Le Guin and Feminist Science Fiction

hook.text: Ursula K. Le Guin imagined a planet with no fixed gender, forcing readers to question everything they assumed about sex.

buildup.text: The Left Hand of Darkness follows a human diplomat on a world where people shift between male and female throughout their lives.

discovery.text: Le Guin used science fiction to conduct thought experiments about society that realistic fiction could never attempt.

twist.text: The literary establishment dismissed science fiction as low art, so her genius was ignored by mainstream critics for decades.

climax.text: Le Guin proved that science fiction was not escapism but the most powerful tool for imagining different social possibilities.

punchline.text: She built other worlds to help us rethink this one.

quiz.question: What is unique about the people on the planet in The Left Hand of Darkness?
options: They communicate telepathically instead of speaking
They shift between male and female throughout their lives
They live for thousands of years without aging

topics.title: Elena Ferrante and Anonymous Genius

hook.text: Elena Ferrante's real identity is unknown. She has never appeared in public, yet her novels sell millions worldwide.

buildup.text: Her Neapolitan Quartet follows two women from childhood in Naples through sixty years of friendship, rivalry, and ambition.

discovery.text: Ferrante coined 'frantumaglia,' a word for the emotional chaos beneath composed surfaces that defines her characters.

twist.text: Journalists investigated her identity, but Ferrante argued that a book should speak for itself without the author's face.

climax.text: Ferrante proved that in an age of celebrity authors, the most powerful literary voice can be one that has no face.

punchline.text: The world's most famous author is someone nobody has met.

quiz.question: What is 'frantumaglia' in Ferrante's literary vocabulary?
options: A type of Italian poetic form
The emotional chaos beneath composed surfaces
The name of the neighborhood where her novels are set

topics.title: Marilynne Robinson's Gilead

hook.text: Marilynne Robinson waited twenty-four years between her first and second novels, and both won major literary prizes.

buildup.text: Gilead is a letter from a dying pastor to his young son, meditating on faith, regret, and the meaning of ordinary life.

discovery.text: Robinson writes about religion with an intellectual depth that makes secular readers take theology seriously as literature.

twist.text: In an era that rewards speed and productivity, Robinson publishes rarely and slowly, insisting that silence is part of writing.

climax.text: Robinson proved that quiet, contemplative fiction about faith can compete with the loudest novels of any generation.

punchline.text: She proved that silence between novels is not absence but depth.

quiz.question: What makes Robinson's approach to publishing unusual?
options: She publishes a new novel every year without fail
She publishes rarely and slowly, insisting that silence is part of writing
She writes under multiple pen names simultaneously

topics.title: Hanya Yanagihara's A Little Life

hook.text: A Little Life is a novel so emotionally devastating that readers form support groups after finishing it.

buildup.text: It follows four college friends in New York, centering on Jude, a man carrying unbearable trauma from his childhood.

discovery.text: Yanagihara deliberately refused to provide redemption or healing, arguing that some wounds do not close in real life.

twist.text: Critics were divided: some called it a masterpiece of empathy, others called it manipulative and gratuitous.

climax.text: The novel proved that fiction can demand radical empathy from readers and refuse to comfort them afterward.

punchline.text: She wrote a novel readers needed support groups to survive.

quiz.question: Why did Yanagihara refuse to provide redemption in the novel?
options: She wanted to write a sequel continuing the story
She argued that some wounds do not close in real life
Her editor demanded a darker ending

topics.title: Ocean Vuong's Poetry and Prose

hook.text: Ocean Vuong's mother could not read, so he wrote her a novel she would never be able to finish — and it became a bestseller.

buildup.text: On Earth We're Briefly Gorgeous is a letter from a Vietnamese American son to his illiterate mother about family and war.

discovery.text: Vuong began as a poet, and his prose carries poetry's intensity, making every sentence feel carved rather than written.

twist.text: He arrived in America at two, speaking no English, and learned the language that would make him one of its finest writers.

climax.text: Vuong proved that literature can bridge the unbridgeable: languages, generations, and the silence between parent and child.

punchline.text: He wrote a masterpiece his mother could never read.

quiz.question: What form does On Earth We're Briefly Gorgeous take?
options: A collection of separate short stories
A letter from a son to his illiterate mother
A traditional three-act novel structure

topics.title: Bernardine Evaristo and Girl, Woman, Other

hook.text: Bernardine Evaristo became the first Black woman to win the Booker Prize, sharing it with Margaret Atwood in 2019.

buildup.text: Girl, Woman, Other weaves twelve interconnected stories of Black British women across generations and identities.

discovery.text: The novel uses a fluid, unpunctuated prose style that mirrors the flowing, overlapping nature of its characters' lives.

twist.text: Evaristo published eight books over decades before winning the Booker, proving that persistence outlasts neglect.

climax.text: She showed that Black British women's stories belong at the center of world literature, not at its margins.

punchline.text: Eight books and decades of work led to one historic night.

quiz.question: What historic distinction did Evaristo achieve with the 2019 Booker Prize?
options: She was the youngest author ever to win the prize
She became the first Black woman to win the Booker Prize
She won for a debut novel

topics.title: The Future of Women in Literature

hook.text: For the first time in history, women now win the majority of major literary prizes worldwide.

buildup.text: From Booker to Pulitzer, women authors have dominated the awards landscape throughout the 2010s and 2020s.

discovery.text: Publishing houses report that women buy roughly eighty percent of fiction sold, shaping the market from both sides.

twist.text: Despite this progress, studies show that books by women still receive fewer reviews and less critical attention than books by men.

climax.text: The revolution women started centuries ago is still unfinished, but the direction is clear: literature's future is female.

punchline.text: Women won the right to write and then won everything else.

quiz.question: What gap still exists despite women's literary success?
options: Women are still banned from submitting to major literary prizes
Books by women still receive fewer reviews and less critical attention than books by men
Women are unable to publish without a male co-author
